info.name: Okta to Anthropic WIF Integration
info.description:
# Okta → Anthropic Workload Identity Federation (WIF)

Call the Claude API **without an API key**. This collection shows the full machine-to-machine flow end to end: an Okta service app gets a short-lived OIDC token, Anthropic exchanges it for a short-lived Claude API token through Workload Identity Federation, and that token calls Claude.

It is a working reference you can run in Postman to:

- **Learn** how WIF works on the wire, one HTTP call at a time.
- **Validate** an Okta + Anthropic WIF setup before you wire it into an application.
- **Troubleshoot** a failing setup, with scripts that decode tokens and explain errors.

> In production you normally don't make these calls yourself. The Anthropic SDKs (Python, TypeScript, Go, Java, C#, Ruby, PHP) take an Okta token provider, perform the exchange, and refresh the token for you. See [Use WIF with Okta](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/manage-claude/wif-providers/okta).

---

## Why Workload Identity Federation?

| Long-lived API key (`sk-ant-api...`) | Workload Identity Federation |
| --- | --- |
| A static secret that must be stored, distributed and rotated | No Anthropic secret at all: the workload proves who it is with its IdP |
| Valid until someone revokes it | Tokens live minutes (60 s to 24 h, set per rule) |
| Hard to tie to a specific workload | Each token maps to a federation rule and a service account, and every exchange is logged in the Claude Console |
| A leaked key works from anywhere | A leaked token expires quickly, and Okta access can be cut off centrally |

With `private_key_jwt`, even Okta holds no shared secret: the workload signs its requests with a private key that never leaves it.

---

## How it works

```
 Workload (Postman)              Okta custom auth server            Anthropic API
 ──────────────────              ───────────────────────            ─────────────
 1. Sign client assertion
    (RS256, private key)
        │
        │  POST /oauth2/{authServerId}/v1/token
        │  grant_type=client_credentials
        │  client_assertion=<signed JWT>
        ├──────────────────────────────────►│
        │                                   │ verify signature with the
        │                                   │ app's registered public key
        │◄──────────────────────────────────┤
        │  access_token (JWT)               
        │    iss = https://{domain}/oauth2/{authServerId}
        │    sub = {client_id}
        │    aud = https://api.anthropic.com
        │
        │  2. POST https://api.anthropic.com/v1/oauth/token
        │     grant_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:jwt-bearer
        │     assertion=<Okta JWT>, federation_rule_id, organization_id, workspace_id
        ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────►│
        │                                    verify JWT via the issuer's JWKS,  │
        │                                    match the federation rule          │
        │◄──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
        │  access_token = sk-ant-oat01-... (acts as the rule's service account)
        │
        │  3. POST https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages
        │     Authorization: Bearer sk-ant-oat01-...
        ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────►│
        │◄──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
        │  Claude's reply
```

| Step | Request | Standard | Saves |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | **Okta - Mint OIDC Token** | OAuth 2.0 client credentials ([RFC 6749 §4.4](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6749#section-4.4)) with `private_key_jwt` client authentication ([RFC 7523 §2.2](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7523#section-2.2)) | `okta_access_token` |
| 2 | **Anthropic WIF - Token Exchange** | JWT bearer grant ([RFC 7523 §2.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7523#section-2.1)) | `anthropic_access_token` |
| 3 | **Claude API - Messages** | Bearer token ([RFC 6750](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6750)) | nothing |

Each request's documentation explains its parameters, scripts and errors.

---

## Prerequisites

### Okta

1. **API Access Management** enabled, so you can use a **custom authorization server**. The built-in `default` server works. The Okta *org* authorization server (`/oauth2/v1/token`) does **not**: Okta doesn't publish its signing keys, so Anthropic can't verify its tokens.
2. An **API Services** app integration (OIDC, machine-to-machine). Note its **Client ID** (`0oa...`).
3. Client authentication set to **Public key / Private key** (`private_key_jwt`), with your public key registered. Note the key's **Key ID** (`kid`).
4. **DPoP turned off** on the app ("Require Demonstrating Proof of Possession"). This collection doesn't send DPoP proofs.
5. On the custom authorization server:
   - **Audience** set to `https://api.anthropic.com`.
   - A **scope** the app can request, for example `anthropic.access`.
   - An **access policy** with a rule that lets this app use the **Client Credentials** grant for that scope.
   - Optionally, **custom claims** you want the federation rule to match on.

### Anthropic (Claude Console)

Go to **Settings → Workload identity** (`platform.claude.com/settings/workload-identity-federation`), choose **Connect workload → Custom OIDC**, and create:

1. **Federation issuer.** Issuer URL `https://{okta_domain}/oauth2/{okta_auth_server_id}` with JWKS mode `discovery`. It must equal the token's `iss` claim exactly, with no trailing slash.
2. **Service account** (`svac_...`), a member of the target workspace.
3. **Federation rule** (`fdrl_...`) that:
   - matches `subject_prefix` = your Okta **Client ID** (exact, no `*`) and `audience` = `https://api.anthropic.com`;
   - targets the service account;
   - is scoped to one workspace (`wrkspc_...`);
   - uses `oauth_scope` = `workspace:developer` (the same access as a workspace API key);
   - sets `token_lifetime_seconds` (the wizard suggests 600).

Also copy your **Organization ID** (a UUID) from **Settings → Organization**.

### Generate the key pair

The simplest option needs no tools: in the Okta app's **Client Credentials → Public keys** section, choose **Add key → Generate new key**. Okta registers the public key and shows the private key **once**: copy it in PEM format. Its **Key ID** is shown next to it.

To generate your own key instead (any OS with OpenSSL, including Git Bash on Windows):

```bash
# RSA 2048 private key
openssl genpkey -algorithm RSA -pkeyopt rsa_keygen_bits:2048 -out okta-wif-private.pem

# Public key to register on the Okta app (Okta accepts PEM or JWK)
openssl pkey -in okta-wif-private.pem -pubout -out okta-wif-public.pem
```

Both private key formats work as is: **PKCS#8** (`-----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY-----`) and **PKCS#1** (`-----BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY-----`). The step 1 script reads both, so you don't need to convert anything or install openssl. Password-protected keys aren't supported.

---

## Setup in Postman

1. **Fork or import** this collection.
2. **Create a Postman environment** (recommended) and add the variables from the table below, with your real values. Environment values take precedence over collection values, so the collection keeps its safe placeholders and your real IDs never end up in it.
3. Make `okta_private_key_pem` a **secret**-type variable and put the key in its **current value** only. Initial values sync to Postman's cloud and are included when you share or export; current values stay on your machine.
4. Select the environment and **run the collection** (Collection Runner, or send requests 1 → 2 → 3 in order).
5. Open the **Postman Console** (View → Show Postman Console) to see what each script logged: the signed assertion's details, the decoded Okta claims, the token's lifetime and Claude's answer.

---

## Variables

### You set these

| Variable | Example / format | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `okta_domain` | `your-org.okta.com` | Yes | Your Okta org domain, without `https://`. |
| `okta_auth_server_id` | `default` or `aus...` | Yes | ID of the custom authorization server. |
| `okta_client_id` | `0oa...` | Yes | Client ID of the API Services app. Also the token's `sub` claim. |
| `okta_key_id` | the key's `kid` | Recommended | Key ID of the public key registered on the app. Sent in the assertion's JWT header. |
| `okta_private_key_pem` | `-----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY-----…` | Yes | Unencrypted RSA private key in PEM format, either **PKCS#8** (`BEGIN PRIVATE KEY`) or **PKCS#1** (`BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY`). Treat as a secret. |
| `okta_scope` | `anthropic.access` | Yes | Scope granted to the app on the authorization server. |
| `anthropic_organization_id` | UUID | Yes | Your Anthropic organization ID (Console → Settings → Organization). |
| `anthropic_federation_rule_id` | `fdrl_...` | Yes | The federation rule to evaluate. |
| `anthropic_workspace_id` | `wrkspc_...` | Conditional | Workspace to scope the token to. Required when the rule covers more than one workspace; leave it empty to let a single-workspace rule pick its own. |
| `anthropic_service_account_id` | `svac_...` | No | The rule's target service account. The rule decides the account; if you set this, it must match. Leave the placeholder to omit it. |
| `anthropic_version` | `2026-10-21` | Yes | Value of the `anthropic-version` header on the Messages call. |
| `claude_model` | `claude-opus-5-5` | Yes | Model used for the test message. |

### The scripts set these (leave them empty)

| Variable | Set by | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `okta_client_assertion` | Step 1 pre-request | Signed RS256 client assertion (valid 5 minutes, single use). |
| `okta_assertion_error` | Step 1 pre-request | Why signing failed, if it did. Step 1's post-response script prints it too. |
| `okta_access_token` | Step 1 post-response | Okta access token (JWT). Cleared after a successful exchange, because each one can be exchanged only once. |
| `okta_token_expires_at` | Step 1 post-response | Expiry of the Okta token (epoch ms). |
| `anthropic_access_token` | Step 2 post-response | Short-lived Claude API token (`sk-ant-oat01-...`). |
| `anthropic_token_expires_at` | Step 2 post-response | Expiry of the Anthropic token (epoch ms). |

Every run starts by clearing all six, so a failed step can never leave an old token behind.

---

### Variable scopes

The scripts read every value with `pm.variables.get`, so you can keep your values in any scope. When the same name exists in more than one, Postman uses the first one it finds, in this order: **local → data (Runner file) → environment → collection → global**. So:

- An **environment** value overrides the collection placeholder. This is the recommended setup.
- A **global** value is ignored while the collection still has a variable with the same name. Put the value in the collection or an environment instead, or delete the collection variable.
- Postman sends the **current value**. If you edit only the *initial* value of an existing variable, the old current value is still used. Use *Reset* or edit the current value too.

The scripts write their results (`okta_client_assertion`, `okta_assertion_error`, the tokens and expiries) as collection variables.

## Scripts at a glance

| Request | Pre-request | Post-response |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Okta | Checks the variables and rejects placeholders, accepts PKCS#8 and PKCS#1 keys, rejects password-protected keys, and signs the RS256 assertion synchronously in plain JavaScript (no npm package). The flow is at the top of the script and the crypto helpers are at the bottom. It logs the exact reason and skips the request if anything is wrong. | Saves the token, decodes it, checks `iss`, `sub` and `aud` against what Anthropic will verify, and explains Okta errors (`invalid_client`, `invalid_scope`, DPoP...). |
| 2. Anthropic exchange | Checks that a fresh Okta token exists, checks the format of every Anthropic ID, and builds the JSON body, leaving out optional fields that are empty. | Saves the token and its expiry, checks the `sk-ant-oat01-` prefix, and explains 400 and 401 errors. |
| 3. Messages | Checks that the Anthropic token exists and hasn't expired. | Finds the text block (it may come after a thinking block), checks `stop_reason`, and logs the reply and token usage. |

---

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Step 1 skipped: "Set these variables…" | Placeholders still in place | Set the variables in your environment. |
| Step 1 skipped: "…is password-protected" | The key is password-protected | Export it again without a password, or generate a new key in Okta. |
| Step 1 skipped: "Could not sign…" | The PEM is incomplete, isn't an RSA key, or is shorter than 2048 bits | Paste the whole key, including the `BEGIN` and `END` lines. The message gives the `BEGIN` line and length the script read. |
| Okta `400 invalid_client`: "A client_id must be provided" | The request went out without a client assertion | Open the Postman Console (View → Show Postman Console) and read the `[Step 1 · Okta client assertion]` lines. No `Pre-request script started` line means Postman has an old copy of the collection: re-import it. |
| Your value seems ignored | A variable with the same name in a higher-precedence scope wins | See *Variable scopes*. Check the **current** value, not only the initial value. |
| Okta `401 invalid_client` | Public key, `kid` or Client ID mismatch, or the app doesn't use `private_key_jwt` | Re-check the key pair registered on the app, and `okta_key_id`. |
| Okta `400 invalid_scope` | Scope missing or not allowed by the access policy | Add the scope and a policy rule for Client Credentials. |
| Okta `invalid_dpop_proof` / `use_dpop_nonce` | DPoP required on the app | Turn DPoP off for this app. |
| Step 1 test: "decoded JWT payload…" | You used the Okta org authorization server, whose tokens Anthropic can't verify | Use a custom authorization server (`default` or `aus...`). |
| Step 1 test: `aud` | Authorization server audience isn't `https://api.anthropic.com` | Change the audience on the authorization server. |
| Anthropic `401 Authentication failed` | Any assertion check failed (the message is deliberately generic) | Open the [authentication history](https://platform.claude.com/settings/workload-identity-federation?tab=history). It names the reason. |
| …reason `jti_reused` | The same Okta token was exchanged twice | Run step 1 again. The collection clears the Okta token after each exchange. |
| …reason `workspace_id_required` | The rule covers several workspaces | Set `anthropic_workspace_id`. |
| …reason `match_subject_prefix` | `sub` ≠ the rule's `subject_prefix` | Set `subject_prefix` to the exact Client ID (it's case-sensitive). |
| …issuer mismatch | `iss` ≠ the issuer URL | The issuer URL must be `https://{domain}/oauth2/{authServerId}`, byte for byte. |
| Anthropic `400 invalid_request_error` | Missing or malformed field | Check the `fdrl_`, UUID and `wrkspc_` formats. |
| Messages `403` | The rule's `oauth_scope` doesn't allow the endpoint | Use `workspace:developer`. |
| Messages `401` | The Anthropic token expired | Run steps 1 and 2 again. |
| Messages `404` | Unknown model | Set `claude_model` to a current model ID. |

---

## Security notes

- Keep the private key out of version control and out of *initial* values. Use a secret-type variable with a current value only.
- Pin the federation rule to one **exact** Client ID. Every service app on the same Okta authorization server shares one issuer, so a rule without `subject_prefix` would trust all of them.
- Keep token lifetimes short. Anthropic caps the minted token at twice the Okta token's remaining lifetime, and at the rule's `token_lifetime_seconds`.
- Give the service account only the workspace it needs, and review the authentication history regularly.

---

## References

- [Workload Identity Federation overview](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/manage-claude/workload-identity-federation)
- [Use WIF with Okta](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/manage-claude/wif-providers/okta)
- [WIF reference: exchange fields, validation rules, errors](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/manage-claude/wif-reference)
- [Okta: implement OAuth for Okta with a service app](https://developer.okta.com/docs/guides/implement-oauth-for-okta-serviceapp/main/)
- [RFC 7523: JWT profile for OAuth 2.0 client authentication and authorization grants](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7523)
- [Claude Messages API](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/api/messages)

*Community reference collection. It isn't an official Anthropic or Okta artifact. Check every configuration against your organization's security standards before using it in production.*

item.name: 1. Okta - Mint OIDC Token
item.description:
## Step 1: Mint an OIDC access token from Okta

Gets a short-lived **JWT access token** from your Okta **custom authorization server** using the OAuth 2.0 **client credentials** grant. The client authenticates with **`private_key_jwt`** ([RFC 7523 §2.2](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7523#section-2.2)): instead of a client secret, it sends a JWT signed with its RSA private key, and Okta verifies it with the public key registered on the app.

This Okta token is the identity that step 2 presents to Anthropic.

---

### Request

`POST https://{{okta_domain}}/oauth2/{{okta_auth_server_id}}/v1/token`, with `Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded`

| Field | Value | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `grant_type` | `client_credentials` | Machine-to-machine grant: no user involved. |
| `scope` | `{{okta_scope}}` | A scope the access policy lets this app request. Okta rejects the request without one. |
| `client_assertion_type` | `urn:ietf:params:oauth:client-assertion-type:jwt-bearer` | Says the client authenticates with a signed JWT. |
| `client_assertion` | `{{okta_client_assertion}}` | The RS256 JWT the pre-request script signs. |
| `client_id` | `{{okta_client_id}}` | Optional with `private_key_jwt`, but it lets Okta name the app in its error if the assertion is rejected. |

> Use a **custom** authorization server (`default` or `aus...`). The Okta org authorization server (`/oauth2/v1/token`) issues tokens Anthropic can't verify.

---

### Signing the client assertion (pre-request script)

This request's **Scripts → Pre-request** tab signs the assertion. It reads top to bottom: a few settings, then `signClientAssertion()` with the whole flow, then helpers (SHA-256, PEM/DER parsing and RSA) at the bottom that you don't need to read.

It signs **synchronously in plain JavaScript** (a built-in SHA-256, and RSA with `BigInt`), with no npm package and no Web Crypto, so it works in every Postman app, plan and runner, including Newman. Synchronous matters: Postman doesn't always wait for promises such as `crypto.subtle` before it sends the request, and the request would then go out with an empty `client_assertion` (Okta answers `invalid_client: A client_id must be provided in the request`).

The script:

1. **Clears** `okta_client_assertion`, `okta_assertion_error`, `okta_access_token`, `anthropic_access_token` and their expiry variables, so a failed run can't reuse an old token.
2. **Validates** the inputs with `pm.variables.get`, so environment, collection and global values all work (see *Variable scopes* in the collection docs). It rejects placeholders, password-protected keys, non-RSA keys and keys shorter than 2048 bits.
3. **Reads the key** in either format, **PKCS#8** (`BEGIN PRIVATE KEY`) or **PKCS#1** (`BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY`), with or without line breaks, so no openssl is needed.
4. **Builds** the JWT:

   | Part | Claim | Value |
   | --- | --- | --- |
   | Header | `alg` / `typ` | `RS256` / `JWT` |
   | Header | `kid` | `{{okta_key_id}}`, if set. Okta needs it when the app has more than one key. |
   | Payload | `iss`, `sub` | `{{okta_client_id}}` |
   | Payload | `aud` | The exact token endpoint URL of this request |
   | Payload | `iat`, `exp` | Now, and now + 5 minutes |
   | Payload | `jti` | A random UUID. Okta rejects a reused `jti`. |

5. **Signs** it with RS256 (RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 / SHA-256), checks the signature against the key's own public part, stores it in `okta_client_assertion` and logs `Signed RS256 client assertion` with the endpoint, Client ID, `kid` and key size.

If anything fails, the script logs the reason in the Postman Console (with the key's `BEGIN` line and length, never the key itself), stores it in `okta_assertion_error`, and **skips the request** (`pm.execution.skipRequest()`). If the request is sent anyway, the post-response script prints the same reason.

---

### Post-response script

- Checks for `200 OK`. On an error, it logs Okta's error with a hint (see the table below). Okta answers in two shapes, OAuth (`error`, `error_description`) or its own API form (`errorCode`, `errorSummary`, `errorId`), and the script reads both. The `errorId` can be searched in the Okta System Log.
- Saves `access_token` → `okta_access_token`, and its expiry → `okta_token_expires_at`.
- **Decodes** the JWT (without verifying the signature) and checks the claims Anthropic will check:
  - `iss` must equal `https://{{okta_domain}}/oauth2/{{okta_auth_server_id}}`. This is the issuer URL you register in the Claude Console.
  - `sub` must equal `{{okta_client_id}}`. This is what the federation rule's `subject_prefix` matches.
  - `aud` must include `https://api.anthropic.com`.
  - A lifetime over 1 hour (Anthropic's default issuer maximum) logs a warning.

The decoded claims are printed in the Console. They're exactly what you need to configure the federation issuer and rule.

---

### Common errors

| Okta error | Meaning | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `invalid_client`: "A client_id must be provided" | The request went out without a client assertion | Read the `[Step 1 · Okta client assertion]` lines in the Postman Console. They give the reason. |
| `invalid_client` | Okta can't verify the assertion | Check the public key on the app, `okta_key_id`, `okta_client_id`, and that the app uses *Public key / Private key*. |
| `invalid_scope` | Scope not granted | Create the scope and allow it in an access policy rule. |
| `unauthorized_client` | Grant not allowed | Use an *API Services* app and allow *Client Credentials* in the policy rule. |
| `invalid_dpop_proof` / `use_dpop_nonce` | The app requires DPoP | Turn off DPoP on the app for this flow. |
| `access_denied` | No policy rule matched | Add a rule for this client and scope. |

exec: // Step 1 pre-request: sign the Okta client assertion
// Okta authenticates the app with a short-lived JWT (RFC 7523, private_key_jwt)
// signed by the app's RSA private key. This script builds that JWT and stores it
// in okta_client_assertion, which the request body sends.
//   2. signClientAssertion(): the whole flow, top to bottom.
//   3. Helpers: SHA-256, PEM/DER parsing and RSA. You don't need to read them.
// Signing is SYNCHRONOUS on purpose: Postman does not always wait for promises
// (such as crypto.subtle) before it sends the request, which would send an empty
// client_assertion. It needs no npm package, so it works in every Postman app,
// Accepts PKCS#8 ("BEGIN PRIVATE KEY") and PKCS#1 ("BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY")
// keys. Any failure is logged, stored in okta_assertion_error, and the request
const ASSERTION_TTL_SECONDS = 300; // Okta accepts at most 1 hour; keep it short.
console.log(LOG + ' Pre-request script started (synchronous RS256 signer).');
// Clear state from earlier runs so a failure here cannot leave stale tokens behind.
// A key pasted from a JSON file may contain literal "\n" sequences; turn them into line breaks.
if (looksLikePlaceholder(authServerId)) problems.push('okta_auth_server_id (for example default or aus...)');
if (looksLikePlaceholder(clientId)) problems.push('okta_client_id (the API Services app Client ID, 0oa...)');
return fail('Set these variables (in the Current value column) before running the collection: ' +
// Describe what was read, without printing the secret, so a wrong value is easy to spot.
return fail('okta_private_key_pem is encrypted (password-protected). Export it without a password ' +
'("BEGIN PRIVATE KEY" or "BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY").');
const isPkcs1 = /-----BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY-----[\s\S]+-----END RSA PRIVATE KEY-----/.test(privateKeyPem);
const isPkcs8 = /-----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY-----[\s\S]+-----END PRIVATE KEY-----/.test(privateKeyPem);
return fail('okta_private_key_pem must be an RSA private key in PEM format, starting with ' +
'"-----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY-----" (PKCS#8) or "-----BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY-----" (PKCS#1) and ending ' +
'with the matching END line. Read: ' + keySummary + '.');
return fail('This Postman version has no BigInt support, which RSA signing needs. Update Postman.');
// The assertion audience must be the exact token endpoint this request calls.
header.kid = keyId; // Needed when the Okta app has more than one public key registered.
jti: randomId() // Okta rejects a reused jti.
return fail('Could not sign with okta_private_key_pem: ' + (e && e.message ? e.message : e) + '. ' +
'Read: ' + keySummary + '. Check that it is an unencrypted RSA key and that the whole PEM was pasted.');
// ---- 3. Helpers (no need to read past this line) ----------------------------
// pm.variables resolves the current value of local, data, environment,
// collection and global variables, in that order of precedence.
// Stop the request from being sent with a missing or broken assertion.
const rotr = function (x, n) { return (x >>> n) | (x << (32 - n)); };
for (let t = 0; t < 16; t++) W[t] = view.getUint32(offset + t * 4);
const t1 = (h + S1 + ch + K[t] + W[t]) | 0;
for (let i = 0; i < 8; i++) outView.setUint32(i * 4, H[i] >>> 0);
for (let i = 0; i < bytes.length; i++) binary += String.fromCharCode(bytes[i]);
for (let i = 0; i < 32; i++) id += Math.floor(Math.random() * 16).toString(16);
throw new Error('the text between the PEM header and footer is not valid base64');
for (let i = 0; i < binary.length; i++) bytes[i] = binary.charCodeAt(i);
// Reads one DER TLV at pos and returns { tag, start, end } of its contents.
if (pos + 2 > bytes.length) throw new Error('the key is truncated');
if (count < 1 || count > 4) throw new Error('unsupported DER length');
for (let i = 0; i < count; i++) length = length * 256 + bytes[start + i];
if (start + length > bytes.length) throw new Error('the key is truncated');
return { tag: tag, start: start, end: start + length };
if (node.tag !== 0x30) throw new Error(what + ' is not a DER SEQUENCE');
for (let i = start; i < end; i++) hex += bytes[i].toString(16).padStart(2, '0');
// PKCS#1 RSAPrivateKey: SEQUENCE { version, n, e, d, p, q, dp, dq, qinv, ... }
const seq = readSequence(bytes, offset, 'the RSA private key');
if (node.tag !== 0x02) throw new Error('expected an INTEGER inside the RSA private key');
if (values.length < 9) throw new Error('the RSA private key is missing fields');
return { n: values[1], e: values[2], d: values[3], p: values[4], q: values[5],
dp: values[6], dq: values[7], qinv: values[8] };

item.name: 2. Anthropic WIF - Token Exchange (RFC 7523 JWT bearer)
item.description:
## Step 2: Exchange the Okta token for an Anthropic access token

Presents the Okta JWT from step 1 to Anthropic's token endpoint. Anthropic verifies the token's signature with the Okta issuer's published keys (JWKS), checks it against your **federation rule**, and returns a short-lived Claude API access token (`sk-ant-oat01-...`) that acts as the rule's **service account**. No Anthropic API key is involved.

The endpoint uses the OAuth 2.0 **JWT bearer grant** from [RFC 7523 §2.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7523#section-2.1), as documented in Anthropic's [WIF reference](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/manage-claude/wif-reference#token-exchange-request).

> **Run step 1 first.** Each Okta token can be exchanged **only once**: Anthropic rejects a reused `jti` as a replay. The collection clears `okta_access_token` after a successful exchange, so send step 1 again before you send step 2 again.

---

### Request

`POST https://api.anthropic.com/v1/oauth/token`, with `Content-Type: application/json`

| Field | Required | Value | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `grant_type` | Yes | `urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:jwt-bearer` | Always this value. |
| `assertion` | Yes | `{{okta_access_token}}` | The Okta JWT from step 1 (at most 16 KiB). |
| `federation_rule_id` | Yes | `{{anthropic_federation_rule_id}}` | The `fdrl_...` rule to evaluate. |
| `organization_id` | Yes | `{{anthropic_organization_id}}` | Your Anthropic organization UUID. |
| `service_account_id` | No | `{{anthropic_service_account_id}}` | The rule's target `svac_...` account. The rule decides the account; if you send this, it must match. |
| `workspace_id` | Conditional | `{{anthropic_workspace_id}}` | The `wrkspc_...` workspace to scope the token to. Required when the rule covers more than one workspace. |

### What Anthropic verifies

- **Signature:** an asymmetric algorithm (RS256 from Okta), and a `kid` that is in the issuer's JWKS.
- **Issuer:** `iss` equals the registered issuer URL exactly.
- **Claims:** `sub`, `iat` and `exp` present; `exp` in the future, with 30 s of leeway; lifetime within the issuer maximum (1 h by default).
- **Rule match:** `subject_prefix`, `audience`, `claims` and any CEL `condition` on the rule.
- **Replay:** the `jti` hasn't been exchanged before.

---

### Pre-request script

- Stops with a clear message if `okta_access_token` is missing or expired.
- Checks the format of each ID: `fdrl_...`, a UUID for the organization, `svac_...`, `wrkspc_...`. Placeholders count as unset.
- **Builds the JSON body** and leaves out optional fields that are empty. An empty `workspace_id` would otherwise be rejected. The body below is the template; the script sends the cleaned-up version.
- Clears any previous `anthropic_access_token`.

### Post-response script

- Checks for `200 OK`, a `Bearer` token type, an `access_token` that starts with `sk-ant-oat01-`, and a positive `expires_in`.
- Saves `anthropic_access_token` and `anthropic_token_expires_at`, and logs the granted `scope` and the expiry.
- Clears the spent Okta token.
- On an error, logs the `request-id` and a hint.

### Response

| Field | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `access_token` | The short-lived Claude API token, `sk-ant-oat01-...`. Send it as `Authorization: Bearer`. |
| `token_type` | Always `Bearer`. |
| `expires_in` | Lifetime in seconds: the rule's `token_lifetime_seconds`, capped at twice the Okta token's remaining lifetime, and never below 60. |
| `scope` | The OAuth scope from the rule, for example `workspace:developer`. |

---

### Errors

| Status | Cause | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `400 invalid_request_error` | Missing or malformed field (rule ID, workspace ID…) | The message names the field. Fix the variable. |
| `401 authentication_error` "Authentication failed" | Any verification failed. The message is generic on purpose, so callers can't probe the rule's configuration. | Open the [authentication history](https://platform.claude.com/settings/workload-identity-federation?tab=history) to see the reason, such as `match_subject_prefix`, `workspace_id_required` or `jti_reused`. |

A `401` with no matching entry in the authentication history usually means Anthropic didn't recognize the `federation_rule_id`.

item.name: 3. Claude API - Messages (/v1/messages)
item.description:
## Step 3: Call Claude with the federated token

Sends a one-line prompt to the [Messages API](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/api/messages) using the token from step 2. A `200` with a text answer proves the whole chain works: Okta identity → Anthropic federation → Claude API access, with **no API key anywhere**.

> The token is sent as `Authorization: Bearer {{anthropic_access_token}}`. A federated token replaces the `x-api-key` header; don't send both.

---

### Request

`POST https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages`

| Header | Value | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Authorization` | `Bearer {{anthropic_access_token}}` | The `sk-ant-oat01-...` token from step 2. |
| `anthropic-version` | `{{anthropic_version}}` | API version (`2026-10-21`, as in Anthropic's WIF examples). |
| `Content-Type` | `application/json` | |

| Body field | Value | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `model` | `{{claude_model}}` | Defaults to `claude-opus-5-5`. Any model your workspace can use works. |
| `max_tokens` | `1024` | Upper bound on the reply length. |
| `output_config.effort` | `low` | This is a short smoke test, so low effort keeps it fast and cheap. Remove it to use the model's default. |
| `messages` | One user message | Asks Claude to confirm that WIF authentication works. |

---

### Pre-request script

Stops with a clear message if `anthropic_access_token` is missing or expired, or if `claude_model` is empty, instead of sending a call that would fail with `401`.

### Post-response script

- Checks for `200 OK`. On an error, logs the error type, message, `request-id` and a hint.
- Checks that `type` is `message` and that `stop_reason` is a normal completion. A `refusal` is logged with its `stop_details`.
- Finds the **text** content block. Current models think adaptively, so a `thinking` block can come before the text, and the script doesn't assume `content[0]` is text.
- Logs the model's reply and the token usage to the Postman Console.

---

### Errors

| Status | Error type | Likely cause | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `400` | `invalid_request_error` | Bad body or a parameter the model doesn't accept | Check the body and `claude_model`. |
| `401` | `authentication_error` | Token expired or invalid | Run steps 1 and 2 again. |
| `403` | `permission_error` | The rule's `oauth_scope` doesn't allow `/v1/messages` | Use `workspace:developer` on the federation rule. |
| `404` | `not_found_error` | Unknown model | Set `claude_model` to a current model ID. |
| `429` | `rate_limit_error` | Workspace rate limit reached | Wait for the `retry-after` delay. |
| `529` | `overloaded_error` | API temporarily overloaded | Send again in a moment. |

### Next steps

In an application, let the Anthropic SDK handle steps 2 and 3: give it a function that returns a fresh Okta token, and it exchanges and refreshes the Anthropic token automatically. See the language examples in [Use WIF with Okta](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/manage-claude/wif-providers/okta#acquire-a-token-and-call-the-claude-api).
